newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary "on track" for economic growth -ING Baring.
newsitem.headline: Hungary "on track" for economic growth -ING Baring.

text.p: Hungary is back on track to resume economic growth in 1997 while maintaining tight monetary policies after two years of stagnation, ING Barings said.

"In our view, increased political consensus and determination to remain on track with economic reforms should continue in 1997/98 and Hungary could potentially join the ranks of the 'soaring eagles' of Central and Eastern Europe," ING Barings said in a research report on Hungary.
It said GDP growth would be driven by "higher export growth, a moderate recovery in private consumption and stronger investment".
But the report cautioned that "over the medium term, the Hungarian economy shows considerably lower growth prospects than other Visegrad countries.
"Despite annual productivity growth of over 10 percent, low domestic savings and investment ratios, in addition to reduced public spending, continue to limit the country's growth potential."
The securities firm said that after a drop in real GDP growth to 0.5 percent in 1996, the economy could grow by a moderate two percent in 1997 and 3.5 percent in 1998.
At the same time, a shock austerity programme introduced in March 1995 to tackle inflation, soaring budget deficits and the current account deficit, has begun to bear fruit, ING Barings said.
It predicted that year-on-year inflation would be just below 20 percent for 1996 and could dip to 16 percent in 1997.
Meanwhile, as economic growth recovers, the current account deficit could grow from 4.0 percent of GDP in 1996 to 4.8 percent of GDP in 1997. @

"Improvements in the invisibles will partially offset the widening trade deficit, which is expected to increase to 5.7 percent of GDP in 1997 from 5.1 percent of GDP in 1996," the report said, citing growth in tourism as a major contributor to improvements in the current account.

The report said cuts in government spending were in part offset by high social security costs. It also said Hungary's spending targets for this year would be adversely affected by a 50 billion forint transfer from the government to the central bank to compensate for losses related to the bank's sterilisation actitivities. @

"Offsetting these items, however, will be higher-than-expected corporate and import tax receipts in the central budget which, supported by a relative improvement in the cost of debt servicing, will result in a central budget deficit of 150-170 billion forints, well below the targeted 232 billion."

The report said Hungary's competitiveness within the region, which had been cast into doubt by relatively high wages, had been restored by a cumulative real wage fall of 15 percent since early 1995. @
